meta.description: Surco gets your DJ tracks ready in seconds. Convert between AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC and MP3 in any direction, edit tags and metadata from Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer, Beatport and MusicBrainz, and send your tracks to Apple Music, rekordbox, Engine DJ or Traktor. And catch re-encoded MP3s disguised as lossless.

features.title: Every step, from download to the booth
features.lede: What Surco does, one line per feature. Open any of them for the full detail.

items.s: AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC and MP3 in any direction, and it also reads M4A, AAC, OGG and OPUS.
items.d: AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC or MP3, in any direction. FLAC to MP3 so it fits on the USB stick, WAV to AIFF to carry the artwork, MP3 to whatever your DJ app asks for. It also reads M4A, AAC, OGG and OPUS. An M4A can stay as it is; the other three always transcode.

items.t: No re-encode when it isn't needed
items.s: If the file is already in that format, it is copied as is instead of re-encoded.
items.d: A file already in the format is copied byte for byte unless your quality settings or an audio filter change its audio; on MP3 and AIFF over APFS it is an instant clone at any size.

items.s: Pick bitrate, bit depth and sample rate, or keep the source's.
items.d: MP3 bitrate, bit depth and sample rate. By default the source's are kept, except 16-bit audio padded to 24, which is saved as true 16-bit with no loss.

items.s: A 16-bit rip never ends up at 24 unless you ask.
items.d: Pin the depth so a 16-bit rip never quietly comes out at 24.

items.s: Every track at the same volume, with a limiter only when there is no other way.
items.d: One constant gain, and a limiter only when the target cannot be hit otherwise.

items.t: It tells you what it will do first
items.s: Before converting you see how far each track will move and whether the limiter steps in.
items.d: How far this track will move, whether the limiter steps in, and by how many decibels the peaks would overshoot.

items.s: Trims silence at the start and end, with the cut visible on the wave.
items.d: The cut visible on the wave, with millisecond nudging.

items.s: A folder, beside the original, Apple Music, rekordbox, Engine DJ or Traktor.
items.d: A folder, beside the original or Apple Music. And in rekordbox, Engine DJ and Traktor you choose whether the track gets updated or added too.

items.s: Brings upsampled or padded files back to 44.1 and 16-bit, and leaves genuine ones untouched.
items.d: The "Corrected" mode rewrites at 44.1 only the tracks measured as upsampled; genuine and unverifiable files come out untouched. And "Corrected" bit depth saves 16-bit audio padded to 24 as true 16-bit, losslessly; "same as source" keeps the container as it is.

groups.title: Tag
groups.replaces: instead of five websites and a tag editor

items.s: Finds artist, album, year, BPM, key, label and catalogue number across five sources.
items.d: Artist, album, year, BPM and key. Label and catalogue number come from Discogs, Beatport and MusicBrainz, and Beatport adds the mix and the ISRC.

items.s: Tells each cut apart by its length, even when the title doesn't help.
items.d: By track length, which tells two cuts apart when the title cannot.

items.s: Applies only high-confidence matches and leaves the doubtful ones for you to confirm.
items.d: Works through the whole list, applies only high-confidence matches and leaves the doubtful ones for you to confirm. If you applied the wrong release, ⌘Z brings back the tags of every track in it.

items.s: Edit a whole release's fields at once, with find and replace.
items.d: The fields a release shares, plus find and replace with regex.

items.s: Fetches artwork from any source or uses yours, cropped to your liking.
items.d: From Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer, Beatport, MusicBrainz or your own, with square cropping and a size cap you set.

items.s: Writes the tag version CDJs and rekordbox read without surprises.
items.d: So CDJs and rekordbox read it without surprises.

items.s: Your star ratings are read and written the way Traktor and Windows understand them.
items.d: In both frames Traktor and Windows Media Player read. And the stars you already set in Traktor show up here.

items.s: Style, country, media type and release URL, under the names mp3tag uses.
items.d: Style, country, media type and the release URL, under the names mp3tag uses so they never double up.

items.s: Create the field you are missing and use it in the editor and in file names.
items.d: Create the field you are missing with a name and a key, and use it in the editor, in the file name and in find and replace. It is saved in every format.

items.t: The full date, if you want it
items.s: Saves the full date, like 2020-12-01, when the source has it.
items.d: Year as 2020-12-01 when the file or Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer, Beatport or MusicBrainz carry the whole date. File names and rekordbox still get the year alone.

items.s: Several genres on one track, with the separator you prefer.
items.d: Each list picks its own separator: comma, semicolon, slash or one of yours. Editing several tracks, each tag says whether it is on all of them or some.

items.t: You decide what a match touches
items.s: A switch per field so a match never overwrites what you set by hand.
items.d: A switch per field: the genre you set by hand survives applying a release.

items.s: See the tags other programs left behind and remove the ones you don't need.
items.d: Inspect them and remove them one by one, or wipe the whole sheet.

items.s: Catches MP3s posing as FLAC or WAV.
items.d: Draws the spectrum with the codec cut marked on the image.

items.s: Tells apart transcodes, regenerated treble and fake hi-res.
items.d: A transcode, possible treble regenerated by an enhancer, and hi-res that was a stretched 44.1.

items.s: Calibrated against 6000 real tracks so a dull master never counts as a fake.
items.d: It checks there is a real cut first, a cliff inside one kilohertz: a dull master is not a fake. Calibrated against 6000 real lossless tracks.

items.s: Every verdict comes with the measurements behind it.
items.d: Every verdict comes with the measurement behind it: how far the energy reaches, where the cutoff sits and how much it drops within one kilohertz.

items.t: An MP3 is not a defect
items.s: An MP3 is graded as an MP3 and comes out clean when it is.
items.d: Its cut is the format, not a flaw: it is graded on its own scale and comes out clean when it is.

items.s: Loudness, peaks, dynamics, balance and noise floor, colour-coded.
items.d: LUFS, true peak, dynamics, L/R balance and noise floor.

items.s: Marks clipping with the same threshold as Audacity.
items.d: Same sample-by-sample threshold, so the red marks agree with theirs.

items.s: Zooms the waveform up to 256 times without pixelating.
items.d: Re-decodes the visible slice instead of stretching pixels.

items.s: Removes vinyl clicks, noise and rumble, and lets you compare before and after.
items.d: Clicks, background noise and rumble, with a gapless A/B to hear what it took.

items.s: Works out BPM and key from the audio and suggests them for you to confirm.
items.d: From the audio itself, always as a suggestion you confirm.

items.s: Tells you if a track is already in your Apple Music or Engine DJ.
items.d: Tells you if a track is in your Apple Music or Engine DJ, and filters the rest.

items.s: Checks whether a 24-bit file really is 24-bit.
items.d: A declared 24-bit file is verified against its own samples: if almost no sample in the first minute uses the low byte, it is 16-bit audio padded out. It isn't a defect, it sounds the same, and with explanations on you see the measured share.

items.s: Open and organise your rekordbox playlists without leaving Surco.
items.d: Open them in Surco with their folders and in their order, with rekordbox's waveform and cues on every track. And organise them from here. Create, rename and delete playlists and folders, drag them to move them, add, remove and reorder tracks, and pick in the editor which playlists each track is in. If rekordbox is open, the changes wait for you to close it. «Recently added» comes first, with what you added to the collection in the last 30 days, then «All tracks», with your whole collection, including what is in no playlist. If you don't use rekordbox or Apple Music, hide that source. And if you have a set's tracklist, paste it onto a playlist with “Paste tracklist…” and Surco looks each line up in your collection, shows you what it found and adds the tracks in the set's order. In Traktor and Serato too.

items.s: Builds a session from your playlists, your combos, what you like most and harmonic mixing.
items.d: Open it from the command palette, from a folder's menu or on an empty playlist. Choose how long it lasts and which playlists the tracks come from, and say what each one holds, Instrumentals, Vocals or Mixed, for a whole folder too. Surco brings together the pairs you repeat in your sets and tracklists, the tracks with the most stars and plays, Camelot harmonic mixing if you want it and room for what's new, and it counts the time each track plays, not the whole file. Under each track you see why it is there and swap it for another that fits. It learns from your sets how far you move the tempo and how much the key matters to you, keeps your closing tracks for the end, plays the ones you always play more often and opens with a vocal. Lock the tracks you want to keep when you redo it, or start it from a track with its menu. In rekordbox, Traktor and Serato, with the program closed.

items.s: Set hot cues on rekordbox's waveform, by hand or with your marking flow.
items.d: Hot cues A to H and CALLs, on rekordbox's waveform and grid. Drag them, they snap to the bar or the beat, and you can undo. Zooming in shows every beat in detail, measured from the audio itself, and Play starts at once. Pick a flow, like Mix in 64, Mix in 32 or one of your own built from blocks or learned from your collection, and hovering over the waveform shows a ghost of what it would place. One click places it and tells you what doesn't fit. Auto mark suggests where each track drops, on several at once too. It learns how you mark from the cues you already placed and the ones you save, and sets what it's sure of apart from what it doubts. And if you mark the CALLs in rekordbox, Surco places your flow's hot cues when you close it. On a track rekordbox hasn't analyzed yet you work on Surco's grid, and once rekordbox analyzes it, your cues move onto its own. Letters follow track order, and if each letter is a fixed pad for you, turn it off in Settings. If the same track is in Traktor or Engine DJ, saving places the flow there too, on its grid and around its cues. Written to rekordbox after a backup.

items.s: Pulls out the tracks whose cues don't land on the grid's beat.
items.d: When you open them, the editor tells you which cues are off and by how much, and “Onto the beat” moves them onto their beat in one go. In rekordbox, Traktor and Engine DJ, Surco measures every cue against the track's grid and tells you how many tracks drift. You choose how many ms counts in the cue settings, 5, 10 or 20 ms. 10 by default.

items.s: Fix a track's beat grid by hand or with Auto, and the “Bad grid” filter tells you which ones.
items.d: With the cues section maximized you move the grid, change the BPM, put the downbeat at the playhead or hit “Auto”, which fits it to the beats, and see how far it is off here and at the end of the track. “Pin” (G) fixes it on the beat nearest the playhead, or right at the playhead with ⇧. A second pin far from the first counts the beats between them and gives the exact BPM, and in rekordbox a third one opens a stretch with its own tempo. Six checks under the whole-track wave tell you whether it stays on the kick all through the track, and clicking one takes the playhead to that beat. Auto gives the same answer from anywhere in the track and takes the kick from the grid your program analyzed, so it never shifts the grid half a beat onto the offbeat. It saves to rekordbox, Traktor and Engine DJ, and in rekordbox also in stretches with their own tempo. The “Bad grid” filter pulls out the tracks whose grid misses the beats. In Traktor and Engine DJ, for now, for WAV, AIFF and FLAC, and in Traktor also for MP3s made with iTunes. Surco leaves the grid it saves locked, and also saves over one that was already locked in the program.

items.s: After converting, the track stays the same in rekordbox, with its playlists and cues.
items.d: After converting, the track is still the same track in rekordbox, with its playlists, cue points and history, and editing its tags never renames the file. Turn it on in Settings. It backs up first, and if rekordbox is open it waits for you to close it.

items.t: A USB stick for your CDJs
items.s: Prepares a USB stick for your CDJs with cues, grid and waveforms.
items.d: Export your rekordbox playlists to a USB stick with their cues, grid and waveforms, and rekordbox can keep syncing it. Needs rekordbox closed. On macOS and Windows. Also from your Serato crates and Traktor playlists, with their cues, loops and grid, without going through rekordbox.

items.s: Organise your Traktor playlists and set hot cues with the same editor.
items.d: Open them in Surco, organise them as you do rekordbox's and set hot cues on their tracks with the same editor, Auto mark included. Traktor gets them in blue, on buttons 2 to 8, and Surco asks you to quit it before saving. In the editor you choose which playlists each track goes into, once the collection is confirmed in Settings. And if Traktor didn't have it, Surco adds it to your collection when it converts it, cover art included.

items.s: Updates your Traktor collection with a backup first.
items.d: Updates the .nml with a backup first that you restore from Backups, and one write per batch. Needs Traktor closed.

items.s: Traktor cue points survive any conversion.
items.d: Intact across MP3, AIFF, FLAC and WAV, in any combination. Trim and the grid re-anchors by phase.

items.t: Mixed In Key cues, and the MP3 offset
items.s: Brings Mixed In Key cues to Traktor and makes up for the MP3 offset.
items.d: Mixed In Key's cues are translated to Traktor's on conversion. And going from MP3 to another format, or the other way round, Surco makes up for the codec's offset so they land where you see them.

items.s: Open your Engine DJ playlists, set hot cues and export them to a USB drive.
items.d: Open them in Surco and set hot cues on their tracks with the same editor, Auto mark included. Not CALL points, since Engine DJ keeps only hot cues. And export them to a USB drive with its Engine library, ready for the player. In the editor you pick which playlists each track goes in, and if Engine DJ didn't have it, Surco adds it to your library when you convert it.

items.s: Brings artwork, rating and playlist into your Engine DJ library.
items.d: Artwork, rating and playlist in your library. It backs it up first, and won't touch it while Engine is open.

items.s: Exports playlists for rekordbox, Serato and M3U8.
items.d: Paths and metadata, no cues, no ratings. Serato's crate, paths only.

items.s: Adds your tracks to Apple Music with tags and artwork, even on WAV.
items.d: With tags and artwork, even on WAV. macOS only, and never FLAC: Music cannot take it.

items.s: A better copy takes the old one's place in Apple Music and rekordbox, playlists included.
items.d: Load another copy of a track you own, in any format including the same one, and it takes the old one's place in Apple Music and rekordbox, instead of leaving you with two. The track stays in its playlists, with no adding it back to each one by hand, and in Apple Music it keeps its play count and your rating. The Apple Music badge shows what format your copy is in, so you know whether it's worth it.

items.t: Typos and duplicates in your library
items.s: Finds typos, invisible characters and duplicate tracks in your library.
items.d: Groups what your Apple Music library or your list spells more than one way, invisible characters and the tracks you have twice. Each fix reaches the file, Apple Music and, if you sync them, rekordbox, Engine DJ and Traktor, with a backup before writing that you restore from Backups, and Undo. The copy you remove hands its playlists to the one you keep. Apple Music on macOS only.

items.t: Bring in an Apple Music playlist
items.s: Open an Apple Music playlist and work directly on its files.
items.d: Load the playlist and work on its files. It keeps their format and fills in what only lives in Music, like the grouping, also on tracks you open on their own. macOS only.

items.s: Writes the grouping where Apple Music reads it.
items.d: It writes that into its own frame, invisible to almost every other tool.

items.s: Watches your download folders and offers you every new track.
items.d: The folders you load stay watched, and when a new track lands Surco offers it to you without dragging anything again.

items.s: Filters duplicates, failed conversions and matches waiting for you to confirm.
items.d: Filter the duplicates (the same song as a FLAC and an MP3), the ones that failed to convert and the matches waiting for you to confirm.

items.s: Names files and titles with templates like {artist} - {title}.
items.d: Files and titles from {artist} - {title}. A slash inside a field never makes a folder, and if your NAS chokes on accents, accent-free file names.

items.s: Puts artwork and metadata in a WAV, which can't hold them on its own.
items.d: Which on its own holds neither artwork nor metadata.

items.s: Keeps a copy of rekordbox, Traktor and Engine DJ before writing to them.
items.d: Before writing to rekordbox, Traktor or Engine DJ, Surco keeps a dated copy and holds on to the last 5 for each program. Backups, at the bottom of the left sidebar, shows them per program and restores any one in a click: it asks you to close the program, keeps a copy of how it was so you can go back, and drops only that library's waiting changes.

items.s: Keeps the files it replaces or renames so you can restore them.
items.d: The files Surco replaces or renames are kept in Backups › Music files; restore them from there or from the track's backup mark. You choose always, only when the audio changes, or never. By default for 7 days or up to 2 GB. If the disk drops below 5 GB free, the oldest go first.

items.s: Whatever you remove goes to the Trash, or to Backups if the disk has none.
items.d: Whatever you remove goes to the system Trash. On a disk with no Trash, like a NAS, and on Windows, it goes to Backups › Music files, where you can restore it. If you choose Never in Settings → Output, it is deleted for good, and the dialog says so before you confirm.

items.s: Edits save themselves, even if the app dies without warning.
items.d: Edits save themselves: the session comes back even if the app dies mid-crate.

items.t: Checks the copy before trusting it
items.s: It never trusts a conversion that was only half written.
items.d: A half-written file declares the same duration as the whole one. Surco compares what it promises against what actually plays, and never publishes a truncated conversion.

items.s: Repairs, on a copy, the header other apps choke on.
items.d: The header other apps choke on, repaired on a copy. Your file is never touched.

install.lede: Download it for your system or install it with Homebrew. Either way, it updates itself.

items.q: Is it really free?
items.a: Yes. Surco is free and complete: no account, no subscription, no limits. If it saves you hours, you can support its development with a donation.

items.q: Is it a tag and metadata editor?
items.a: Yes, and more. Surco edits your music's tags and metadata (artist, title, album, year, artwork…) and fills them in from Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer, Beatport or MusicBrainz. But it also converts between AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC and MP3 in any direction, checks audio quality and organizes your library: what you'd do with a tag editor and three other apps, in one.

items.q: Does it touch my original files?
items.a: It depends on whether the format changes. Convert to a different format and the original is left alone, with the copy going to a separate folder (Music/Surco). There are two exceptions. If the new copy replaces the old one in your library, Surco removes the old file as soon as it has checked the new one is fine, sending it to the Trash or to Backups. And with “Edit the original” the file is rewritten in place, so changing the format deletes the original. Re-export to the same format and Surco rewrites that file where it is, which is how it updates the tags without re-encoding the audio. When the audio changes (converting, normalizing, trimming), Surco first keeps a backup of the original that you can restore from the track itself; in Settings → Output you choose whether to keep one always, only when the audio changes or never, and for how many days and how much space.

items.q: Does it keep cue points?
items.a: Traktor's do. They survive between MP3, AIFF, FLAC and WAV in any combination, because Surco reads the tree Traktor stores inside the file and writes it back in the target format. Only ALAC loses them, because it has nowhere to keep it. rekordbox and Engine DJ cues live in their library and stay with the track if you update that library when you convert. If you trim silence, the cues shift by what you cut, the beatgrid included (it's re-anchored by phase so it doesn't drift), and anything that can't be re-anchored reliably is dropped rather than left pointing at the wrong beat. Surco warns you before you convert.

items.q: Can I trim the silence off my rips?
items.a: Yes. Surco detects the silence at the head and the tail and shows you both cuts on the waveform, with zoom and millisecond nudges, so you can hear how it lands before applying anything. Trim one track or a whole selection at once. Note that trimming re-encodes the audio, so check the cue point answer above.

items.q: What about vinyl clicks and noise?
items.a: Surco detects them and interpolates them away as it converts, with four strengths. It marks every click it finds on the waveform so you can jump from one to the next, and it renders the repaired track so you can A/B it against the original while it plays, with no gap in the audio. So you hear whether the repair took the clicks out, and whether it took some of the music with them. It also lowers the record's background noise, the hiss and the platter rumble, on its own four-step ladder. It doesn't touch the music in any way you would notice, and on a clean track it changes nothing. It ships off.

items.q: My library is full of MP3s. Can I move them to lossless without losing my playlists?
items.a: Yes, that's what replacing does. Load the AIFF or FLAC of the same track and, if Surco finds it in your library, the button reads “Replace” instead of “Add”. When you convert, the Apple Music entry stops pointing at the MP3 and points at the new file, and in rekordbox the same row is repointed. It keeps its playlists and its cue points, because rekordbox links by track rather than by path. One caveat: rekordbox analyzes the new file and may move the beatgrid, so check the grid afterwards. rekordbox has to be closed to write to its database; Surco offers to close it and backs up first. Once the new file checks out and no program is still using the old one, Surco removes the old one by itself. It goes to the Trash, or to Backups › Music files if it sits on a disk with no Trash, like a NAS. With “Never” chosen in Settings → Output it is deleted for good.

items.q: Does it work with Denon gear (Engine DJ)?
items.a: Yes. In Settings → Output set Engine DJ to “Update and add” and every converted track is registered straight into your Engine DJ library (with its cover, rating and the playlists you pick), ready to sync to your players. It also exports collections to rekordbox, Traktor and Serato.

items.q: Windows says "Windows protected your PC". Is it safe?
items.a: Yes. That's the SmartScreen notice for new apps not yet signed on Windows: click "More info", then "Run anyway". On macOS, Surco is notarized by Apple and opens with no warnings.

items.q: Which formats does it support?
items.a: It converts between AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC and MP3, any to any. Lossless to MP3 to save space, MP3 to AIFF for your DJ app or FLAC to WAV, whatever you need. The quality is yours to pick: MP3 bitrate (320 down to 128 kbps, or VBR V0/V2), bit depth and sample rate. By default they match the source, except 16-bit audio padded to 24, which is saved as true 16-bit with no loss. It also reads M4A, AAC, OGG and OPUS and converts them to any of those five.

items.q: What about broken WAV files?
items.a: Old downloads sometimes carry malformed WAV headers that other apps choke on. Surco repairs them on a temporary copy as it reads (your original is never touched) so the track plays, analyzes and converts normally.

items.q: What if the app closes mid-session?
items.a: You lose nothing. Surco saves your unapplied edits on its own as you work, and on reopening it offers to restore the session with everything just as you left it. Metadata, covers and matches included, even after the machine froze.

items.q: Which languages is it in?
items.a: Spanish, English, German, French, Portuguese (Brazil) and Japanese. It follows your system language by default, and you can pin one in Settings.

items.q: Which systems does it run on?
items.a: macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), Windows and Linux (AppImage). It updates itself, so you'll always have the latest version.

steps.text: From the home page, or with Homebrew on macOS.
In four steps you pick where to look for tags, the output format and folder, and what you do with your tracks. That way the editor only shows what you use.

steps.lead: Tune the rest whenever you like.
steps.text: Everything is in Settings (⌘ ,), and the wizard reopens from the Help menu or ⌘K.

points: Out of the box it analyzes everything on import and searches Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer and MusicBrainz with nothing to set up.
If Surco finds rekordbox, Traktor, Engine DJ or Serato, right after the welcome it asks which one you play with, and the ones you leave unticked stop showing in the sidebar.
sections.shotCaption: The welcome wizard on first launch.

sections.title: Add your tracks
sections.s: Drag in files or whole folders and Surco reads everything on the fly.
body: It reads WAV, FLAC, AIFF, ALAC, MP3, M4A, AAC, OGG and OPUS. The same file never goes in twice.

steps.text: Onto the window, or click “Add files” (⌘O). Surco walks the folders and adds every audio file it finds.
Tracks appear as they're read, with their tags, duration and cover art, so a network folder starts showing right away.

points: A damaged file is flagged and skipped without stopping the import.
If you close the app, it offers to reopen your last session with your unapplied edits.
Surco tells you when new files show up later in the folders you dropped.
sections.shotCaption: Dragging and dropping tracks into the list.

sections.title: Get to know the track list
sections.s: What each row in the list tells you, at a glance.
body: Each row shows the cover art, title, artist and format. Once you analyze quality, the format pill turns green, amber or red.

steps.text: Space plays the selected track in the player at the bottom, with its waveform so you can jump anywhere.

The filters up top (“Doubtful”, “Unconverted”, “Duplicates”, “Silence to trim”…) stay dimmed when no track fits them, and each one tells you how many you will see. Whatever you do next acts only on what you see.
⌘ + click adds tracks and Shift + click picks a range. Delete removes the selection from the list.

points: The ✦ icon marks what Surco filled in on its own, an amber dot what you edited after converting and an undo arrow the tracks with a backup.
You can drag tracks out of Surco into any other app.
⌘K jumps to any track as you type its title or artist.
sections.shotCaption: The track list with filters and statuses.

sections.title: Edit the metadata
sections.s: Every field of the track, minus the leftovers other programs left behind.
body: Select a track and the editor on the right shows its fields, its cover art and its rating.

steps.text: Enter confirms and jumps to the next, and your saved genres and groupings show up as one-click suggestions.
Under BPM and key you see what was measured in the audio itself, ready to apply. If the track has no tags, “Fill from filename” works out the title and artist.

steps.lead: Clean out what the file drags along.
steps.text: “Other metadata” shows the tags other programs left behind, like Serato or ReplayGain leftovers, and you remove them one by one or all at once.

points: Copy and paste metadata between tracks from the context menu. ⌘Z undoes up to twenty steps.
Required fields turn red when they're empty.
The editor sections fold, reorder and hide in Settings → Sections.
sections.shotCaption: The metadata editor with Discogs suggestions.

sections.title: Find the release in your sources
sections.s: Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer, Beatport and MusicBrainz, with details and artwork in one click.
body: Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer and MusicBrainz come switched on and need no account. Beatport is turned on in Settings → Sources.

steps.text: Type the release name or paste a Discogs release id, and press “Search” or the / key.
Each result shows cover art, year, label, catalog number and format. Expand one to see its tracklist. The closest one is flagged “Suggested”.
Click the track and Surco fills in artist, album, year, genre, label, catalog number and cover art in one go.

points: Bandcamp is for self-released and exclusive material, and Deezer for the commercial music Discogs doesn't have.
Beatport needs your account connected (a free one will do) and brings BPM, key, mix and ISRC.
MusicBrainz allows one search per second, so its results can arrive a little later.
With your own Discogs token in Settings you get a higher, faster limit.
sections.shotCaption: Searching a release and picking the track on Discogs.

sections.title: Let Surco tag on its own
sections.s: Every track you drop is looked up and tagged on its own when the match is reliable.
body: Surco compares title, duration, track number and artist against each candidate. An identical title isn't enough, something else has to confirm it.

steps.text: Switch on “Auto-match on import” in Settings. It ships off.
Each one is looked up in the background across your sources and, when the match is reliable, gets its details and cover art.
The ones nothing confirms land in “To confirm”, and you accept them from ⌘K without opening the editor.

points: It never overwrites your work. It skips already-matched tracks and keeps your cover art.
In your libraries' playlists it doesn't search on its own. There the Match button works on the tracks you select.
The “Auto-matched” filter gathers what it did, and the Activity panel explains each verdict.
sections.shotCaption: The Activity panel with the lookups running in the background.

sections.title: Match a whole release
sections.s: Apply a whole release to all its tracks at once.
body: It's for an album or an EP you imported whole.

steps.text: With ⌘ + click or Shift + click. The editor header changes to “Editing N tracks”.
Surco builds a grid with your files on the left and the tracklist on the right, and assigns each one by its duration.
Change any it got wrong from its dropdown and press “Apply to N”.

points: A file that fits no song is left unassigned instead of landing on the wrong one.
For grouping and genre, each tag shows whether it's on all, some or none of them.
If the release isn't in your sources, a command numbers the selection in list order.
sections.shotCaption: Assigning each file to its song and applying to all.

sections.title: Check the real quality
sections.s: See in the spectrum whether a lossless file really is lossless.
body: A genuinely lossless file has sound all the way up the spectrum. An MP3 dressed up as a WAV cuts off sharply, and Surco marks where.

steps.text: Open a track's quality section, or analyze the whole queue with the toolbar button or ⌘⇧A.
Up to about 20 kHz is full quality (green), 18 to 19.5 kHz is doubtful (amber) and below that is bad (red).
Filter the list by “Doubtful”, “Good” or “Unanalyzed” and decide which tracks stay out.

points: An MP3 isn't judged like a lossless file. Its cut is the format, not a flaw.
“Possibly reprocessed” flags highs that look regenerated over an earlier cutoff. It's a measured suspicion, not proof.
Under the spectrum you get LUFS, true peak, dynamics and noise floor, and you can save the report as a PNG.
sections.shotCaption: A track's spectrum with its quality verdict.

sections.title: Clean up your vinyl rips
sections.s: Remove clicks, background noise and the needle's silence at the start and the end.
body: Both sections ship off and apply on conversion. You decide which track needs them.

steps.lead: See how many clicks it has.
steps.text: Surco estimates them and marks them on the waveform, and “Next click” steps through them one by one.
Clicks and background noise have four levels each, from off to strong.
“Hear the result” switches with no gap between the repaired track and the original, so you can hear whether it took some music with it.
The trim section detects the lead-in and the tail, and you fine-tune each cut to the millisecond with its own zoom and preview.

points: Repairing and trimming re-encode the audio. Traktor's cues are kept except on ALAC.
The “Silence to trim” filter gathers the tracks that need it.
Noise is estimated from the track itself, so it works on rips that start right on the music.
sections.shotCaption: Clicks marked on the waveform and background noise in one section.

sections.title: Convert your tracks
sections.s: One track or the whole queue, to the format you pick or in its own.
body: ⌘Enter converts the selected track and ⌘⇧Enter the whole queue, skipping what's already done. If you've filtered the list, only what you see gets converted.

steps.text: In the button's dropdown. AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC or MP3. With “Same as source” each file stays in its format and only the tags are rewritten, instantly.
In Settings → Output. A folder, your Apple Music, next to the original or “Edit the original”.
When it's done you see how many were converted, skipped or failed, and “Show file” takes you to the result.

points: If the conversion changes an original's audio, Surco keeps a backup first. The mark on the row takes you back to it.
With “Edit the original”, changing the format deletes the original.
Converting doesn't search your sources. If you want fresh data, run Match first (⌘⇧D).
sections.shotCaption: The convert button with its format picker.

sections.title: Name and organize the files
sections.s: Files and folders named the way you want.
body: By default Surco keeps the original filename and you decide when to rename.

steps.text: In Settings → Naming click chips like {artist}, {title} or {year}, and a preview shows the result.
A slash creates subfolders, for example {albumArtist}/{album}/{title}.
The editor's regenerate button applies it to one track or the whole selection. If you'd rather not think about it, a setting applies it on conversion.

points: “File names without accents” writes “Royksopp” instead of “Röyksopp”. The tags keep their accents.
Titles can have their own format too, like ({trackNumber}) {title} ({year}), and it's never applied on its own.
sections.shotCaption: The filename template builder in Settings.

sections.title: Take your tracks to your DJ software
sections.s: Apple Music, rekordbox, Engine DJ, Traktor and Serato, while converting or from their playlists.
body: The sidebar shows your libraries. Open any playlist and its tracks join the list with their real files.

steps.text: In Settings → DJ software you decide, for each program, whether it's left alone, gets the tracks it already has updated or also gets the new ones added.
Tracks arrive with their tags and cover art. You can also export the queue as an .xml, .nml or .crate collection, or as an M3U8 playlist.
From the sidebar you create, rename and move playlists and folders by dragging them, without opening the program.

points: If the program is open, Surco waits until you close it or offers to close it, and always keeps a backup before writing.
Traktor doesn't re-read the file, it reads its collection.nml. For it to see your new cues, point Surco at your collection in Settings.
Traktor's cues survive conversion across MP3, AIFF, FLAC and WAV, and are only lost on ALAC.
Load another copy of a track you already have and the button changes to “Replace”, keeping its playlists and cues.
sections.shotCaption: Sending the track to Apple Music or exporting the collection.

sections.title: Mark your cues
sections.s: Hot cues on the rekordbox, Engine DJ or Traktor waveform, with your flow.
body: Open a playlist from any of the three in the sidebar and pick a track. The Cues section shows its waveform and grid.

steps.text: Two come ready-made, Mix in 64 and Mix in 32, and in Settings › Cues Surco learns yours from the cues you already have.
The flow places the rest, counting back. If you'd rather not look for that point, Auto mark suggests it and you accept it with Return.
Surco makes a backup and writes to your collection. If the program is open, it waits until you close it.

points: Auto mark suggests, it doesn't decide. Sure suggestions show a solid line and doubtful ones a dashed line.
With several tracks selected you mark and save them all at once.
Engine DJ and Traktor get the hot cues only. In Traktor they go on buttons 2 to 8, since 1 is its grid.
The “Cues off the grid” filter pulls out the tracks with a cue that misses the beat.
sections.shotCaption: Auto mark suggests where the track drops, with your flow ready to accept.

sections.title: Paste your set's tracklist
sections.s: From a text tracklist to a rekordbox, Traktor or Serato playlist, in the set's order.
body: Any list with one track per line works, with or without times: a YouTube video description, a tracklist copied from a website, or what tracklist prints, the program by Surco's author that identifies the tracks of your own video from YouTube's claims and Shazam (github.com/vigosan/tracklist).

steps.text: Pick “Paste tracklist…”. On a folder, “Playlist from tracklist…” asks for the name.
Surco counts the tracks and gaps it understood. Press “Search in rekordbox”.
Each line shows what Surco found in your collection. Found tracks and other mixes go in; lines that only share the title wait for you to take them.
The tracks go to the end of the playlist in the set's order. Nothing is written before this button.

points: Tracks you don't have are not listed in the review: they are only counted.
If two lines land on the same track, it goes in once.
If rekordbox is open, Surco asks you to close it, as with any playlist change.
Measured on a real 31-track set: 28 went in by themselves and 3 with one click.
sections.shotCaption: The tracklist review before adding: found, doubtful and similar.

sections.title: Build an automatic session
sections.s: A playlist of the length you want, from your combos, your taste and harmonic mixing.
body: Surco orders tracks from the playlists you choose. It joins pairs you repeat in your sets, fits by key and tempo, and leaves room for new tracks.

steps.text: Right-click a folder and pick “Automatic session…”, or “Fill with a session…” on an empty playlist.
Mark each as Instrumentals, Vocals or Mixed, or a whole folder. Mixed ones are your sets, and their order gives the combos.
Alternate instrumental and vocal, combos, taste, Camelot, how long each track plays and new tracks.
Each track says why it is there and “Change” offers others. Redo, adjust or keep it as a normal playlist.

points: Each track counts only the time it plays in the mix, two minutes by default. A real 28-track set lasted an hour.
A combo is a pair that repeats in two or more Mixed playlists. Without them there are none.
New means added in the last 30 days, or with no plays or stars if there are no dates.
It writes to rekordbox, Traktor or Serato with the program closed.
sections.shotCaption: The built session, with its summary, why each track is there and “Change”.

sections.title: Take your playlists on a USB stick
sections.s: Export your playlists to a USB stick ready for the players.
body: It works with rekordbox, Engine DJ, Serato and Traktor playlists, on macOS and Windows.

steps.text: From the USB icon next to the program in the sidebar, from “Export to USB…” in ⌘K or from the notice that shows up when you plug in a stick.

steps.lead: Tick the playlists and the stick.
steps.text: Before copying, Surco tells you how many tracks are new, how many were already there and whether it all fits.
The stick carries the library the players read, with its cues and grid.

points: The music is copied as it is. If your CDJ is an older one, convert anything FLAC or above 24 bits or 48 kHz to AIFF first.
It warns you about a stick in exFAT, NTFS or GPT, which some CDJs can't read.
rekordbox or Engine DJ has to be closed.
sections.shotCaption: Export to USB with the rekordbox playlists.

sections.title: Review your library
sections.s: Typos, spellings and duplicates in your library, all in one place.
body: Changes reach the files, Apple Music and the libraries you sync. Surco keeps a backup before writing, and the review has Undo.

steps.text: It's in the toolbar and goes through your Apple Music, the loaded list or a playlist.
For each case you see what it looks like now and after, and add what you want to the batch.
It's all written in one go.

points: Spellings groups what's written several ways, like DJ Lara and Dj Lara.
Duplicates lets you pick which one stays, and it inherits the other one's playlists.
Damage repairs broken Traktor and Engine DJ cues and durations, and Incomplete proposes how to fill required fields.
BPM, key, cues and rating aren't touched.
sections.shotCaption: Review on a rekordbox playlist, with an extra space in an album name.

sections.title: Shortcuts and settings
sections.s: Nearly everything has a shortcut, ⌘K finds it and Settings holds the rest.
body: Surco is built to work without a mouse.

steps.text: ⌘K finds any action or track, accent-insensitive.
Press ? to see them all. Every button shows its own in its tooltip, and you rebind them in Settings → Shortcuts.
In Settings (⌘ ,) type in “Search settings” and Surco takes you there.

points: ⌘F finds and replaces across every track, and tells you how many it will touch first.
Export your configuration to a file, or point its folder at iCloud Drive or Dropbox to share it across Macs.
Nothing goes through a Surco server. No account, no cloud, no telemetry.
sections.shotCaption: The command palette with search open.

changelog.metaTitle: Surco changelog, What's new in each release
changelog.metaDescription: What's new in each Surco release: Discogs auto-match, rekordbox and Traktor export, loudness analysis, multi-track editing and more.
changelog.title: Everything that has changed in Surco
changelog.lede: The highlights of every release, without the noise. The features that change how you prep your music, version by version.

beta.title: What is coming in the next version
beta.how: To try it now, turn on Get beta versions in Settings, General, and restart Surco. Betas reach the installer from this website, not the Microsoft Store copy.

changelog.outroTitle: Try it all in your next session
changelog.outroLede: Download Surco and prep your first tracks in a couple of minutes.

quality.title: That lossless file was an MP3.
quality.lede: Buying lossless is no guarantee it is. If someone converted an MP3 to FLAC, WAV or AIFF, the file weighs the same but the spectrum shows the wall. Surco flags it before the track ever leaves the house.
quality.goodAlt: Spectrum of a genuine FLAC: energy reaches the top with no cutoff
quality.fakeAlt: Spectrum of an MP3 transcoded to FLAC: empty band above 16 kHz with a straight edge
quality.evidenceGood: No codec cut detected; highs up to ~21.2 kHz.
quality.evidenceBad: Codec cut at ~16 kHz: the source was lossy.

tag.title: The tags, from Discogs, in one click.
tag.lede: Discogs for labels, Bandcamp for self-released, Deezer for the charts, Beatport for the club, MusicBrainz for everything else. One click fills it all in: artist, label, year, BPM and artwork.

batch.title: And it lands in your Apple Music.
batch.lede: Pick a format and a destination and convert the whole folder. With Apple Music and Engine DJ you import nothing: the track shows up in your library with its artwork on, and on Engine DJ, with rating and playlist. Everything else gets the file it expects.

home.heroFree: Free. macOS, Windows and Linux. No account.
home.closeTitle: All of it, in one window.
home.closeNote: No cloud, no limits, nothing to sign up for. It updates itself.
home.closeSafety: Your originals stay untouched: change format and the copy goes to a folder of its own. It only rewrites the file itself if you re-export to the same format, which is how it updates tags without re-encoding. Notarized by Apple.
home.closeSafeRest: When you change format, the copy goes to a separate folder. If the copy replaces the old one in your library, the old one goes to the Trash or to Backups once the new one has been checked. Notarized by Apple.
home.closeStatsRest: Surco doesn’t know who uses it or what you do with your music. The only public figures are the downloads, and they’re in <stats>Stats</stats>.
home.heroLede: Surco converts your tracks, tags them from Discogs or Beatport, checks that your lossless files really are lossless and drops them into rekordbox, Traktor, Engine DJ or Apple Music.

quality.rest: The FLAC you bought may be an inflated MP3.

tag.title: Every tag, in one click
tag.note: Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer, Beatport and MusicBrainz. Artist, label, year, BPM and artwork.
tag.rest: Artist, label, year, BPM and artwork from five sources.

export.title: And they land in your program
export.note: Apple Music, Engine DJ, rekordbox, Traktor or Serato. Nothing to import.
export.rest: It shows up in rekordbox, Traktor, Engine DJ or Apple Music.

replace.title: Upgrade the file. Your playlists never notice.
replace.lede: If the track is already in your Apple Music, the button reads “Replace”. Surco swaps the file and every program points to the new one, so you never add the track back to each playlist by hand.
replace.activityDetail: 1 track now points at the new file

anyFormat.title: MP3 to AIFF, or whatever you like
anyFormat.text: Any format works, the same one included, from a 128 MP3 to a 320.

playlists.title: Playlists, untouched
playlists.text: The track stays in every playlist it was in, cues included.

programs.title: In every program
programs.text: Apple Music, and rekordbox, Engine DJ and Traktor too if you sync them.

sync.title: Change it once. Every program sees it.
sync.lede: Open the track from the Apple Music or rekordbox tab, fix the title, the genre or the file name and press Update tags. Surco carries the change to Apple Music, rekordbox, Traktor and Engine DJ, and it stays the same track in each one.

anyTab.title: From any tab
anyTab.text: Whichever program you open the track from, the change leaves Surco and reaches the others.

sameTrack.title: The same track everywhere
sameTrack.text: Rename the file and every program points to the new one, with its playlists and cues.

waits.title: If it's open, it waits
waits.text: A program that is open gets the change as soon as you close it. Each one with its sync turned on.

cues.title: Mark the drop. The rest of the cues place themselves.
cues.lede: Click where the track drops, or let Auto mark find it. Your flow places the other cues the same way on every track and Surco saves them to rekordbox, Engine DJ or Traktor.

oneClick.title: One click, not eight
oneClick.text: Mark where the track drops and your flow places every other cue.

yourFlow.title: Your flow, not someone else's
yourFlow.text: The cues land where you always put them, the same on every track.

programs.title: Straight to your program
programs.text: rekordbox, Engine DJ and Traktor. Engine DJ and Traktor take the hot cues only.

grid.title: Find the cues that miss the beat.
grid.text: In rekordbox, Engine DJ and Traktor, Surco measures every cue against the grid and pulls out the tracks that drift. Clear them and hit Auto mark. You choose how many ms counts.

review.title: Find the typos and duplicates in your library
review.lede: Surco goes through your Apple Music library, the folder you drop or a rekordbox, Engine DJ or Traktor playlist, and groups what's spelled more than one way, the invisible spaces and characters that sneak in when you copy from a website, and the tracks you have twice. You choose how it should read and the change reaches the files, Apple Music and, if you sync them, rekordbox, Engine DJ and Traktor.

spelling.title: Spellings
spelling.text: DJ Lara and Dj Lara, Head Horny's with two different apostrophes, accents that don't match.

typo.title: Typos
typo.text: Rahcel for Rachel. A typo never joins the batch by itself, you decide.

duplicate.title: Duplicates
duplicate.text: The same track twice. The copy you keep joins the playlists of the one you remove.

everywhere.title: Everywhere
everywhere.text: Files, Apple Music, rekordbox, Engine DJ and Traktor, with a backup of every file and every DJ library, restorable from Backups. And corrections come with Undo.

review.tie: Tied. Pick the one to keep.
review.options: How it is and how it ends up

convert.metaTitle: Convert audio between AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC and MP3 for DJs
convert.metaDescription: Convert in any direction between AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC and MP3, in batches and without losing tags, artwork or Traktor cues. It also reads M4A, AAC, OGG and OPUS. For Mac, Windows and Linux.
convert.lede: FLAC to AIFF for the CDJ, WAV to MP3 so it fits on the USB stick, or MP3 to whatever your DJ app asks for. Surco converts in any direction and carries the tags, the artwork and the Traktor cues along with the audio.
convert.note: macOS, Windows and Linux. No account, no subscription.

example.label: Formats in and out
keeps: Bit depth and sample rate, unless you change them

carry.title: Whatever the file carries makes it to the new format
carry.lede: Each format stores tags its own way. Surco rewrites them in the form the target format expects.

rows.how: Between AIFF, WAV, FLAC and ALAC the samples are the same. For MP3 you pick the quality, from 320 down to 128 kbps or VBR V0/V2.
They take the target format's form, ID3 in AIFF, WAV and MP3, Vorbis comments in FLAC and MP4 atoms in ALAC.
It's embedded in the copy, in a WAV too.
Between MP3, AIFF, FLAC and WAV in any combination, with the MP3 offset compensated. Only ALAC has nowhere to keep them.
If the file is already in that format, it's copied as is and only the tags are rewritten.

why.title: Each format for its own job

items.title: AIFF, the one everything reads
items.text: Lossless, with tags and artwork, and every CDJ and every DJ app reads it.

items.title: MP3, so it fits
items.text: A 320 kbps MP3 takes about a quarter of the space of an AIFF. For a small USB stick or for listening outside the booth.

items.title: FLAC and ALAC, for archiving
items.text: Lossless and compressed, they take up a good deal less than an AIFF. ALAC also plays in Apple Music, and FLAC doesn't.

steps.title: Convert in three steps

items.title: Drop the files
items.text: Drag a file in any format, a selection or a whole folder onto Surco.

items.title: Pick the format
items.text: AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC or MP3, in the menu next to the convert button. With several tracks, also “Same as source”.

items.title: Convert
items.text: The copies go to Music/Surco, next to the original or to Apple Music, and rekordbox, Engine DJ and Traktor are brought up to date if you sync them.

steps.guide: Step by step in the guide

quality.title: Is your lossless really lossless?
quality.lede: An MP3 converted to FLAC, WAV or AIFF weighs the same as the real thing. The spectrum gives it away, because the sound stops at a hard wall. Surco checks every track before you convert it.

items.q: Which formats can I convert?
items.a: In go WAV, FLAC, AIFF, ALAC, MP3, M4A, AAC, OGG and OPUS. Out come AIFF, WAV, FLAC, ALAC and MP3, any to any.

items.q: Do I lose quality when converting?
items.a: Not between lossless formats, because the samples are the same. Going to MP3 loses some, as with any MP3, and you choose how much with the bitrate. Turning an MP3 into an AIFF doesn't bring the quality back, it only makes it bigger.

items.q: Are my originals touched?
items.a: When you change format, the copy goes to a separate folder and the original stays where it was. If the copy replaces the old one in your library, Surco removes the old one once it has checked the new one, to the Trash or to Backups.

items.q: Can I convert a whole folder at once?
items.a: Yes. Drop the folder and convert everything in one go. Conversions run in parallel.

items.q: Does it work on Windows?
items.a: Yes. Surco runs on macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), Windows and Linux.

outro.title: Convert your music
outro.lede: Surco also tags from Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer, Beatport and MusicBrainz and files everything into your library.

flacToAiff.metaTitle: Convert FLAC to AIFF on Mac & Windows, keeping tags and cues
flacToAiff.metaDescription: Batch-convert FLAC to AIFF losslessly for rekordbox, Serato or CDJs. Surco keeps tags, artwork and Traktor cue points, and flags fake FLACs that are really MP3s.
flacToAiff.lede: Drop a folder of FLACs and get AIFFs ready for rekordbox, Serato or older CDJs. The audio stays bit-for-bit lossless, and the tags, artwork and Traktor cue points come across with it.
flacToAiff.note: macOS, Windows and Linux. No account, no subscription.

example.label: Example conversion
example.arrow: lossless, same bit depth and sample rate
keeps: Artist, title, album and every other tag

carry.title: Everything in the FLAC ends up in the AIFF
carry.lede: Online converters hand you the audio and drop the rest. Surco rewrites every tag in the form AIFF expects.

rows.how: Both formats are lossless, so the samples are the same. Bit depth and sample rate are kept.
Vorbis comments become ID3 tags, the ones rekordbox, Serato and Traktor read in an AIFF.
The front cover is embedded in the AIFF.
Surco reads the cue tree Traktor stores in the FLAC and writes it back where Traktor looks for it in an AIFF.
A “24-bit” FLAC that really holds 16 bits is saved as true 16-bit, with no loss.

why.title: Why DJs convert FLAC to AIFF

items.title: Older players skip FLAC
items.text: The CDJ-2000NXS and older Pioneer players don't read FLAC from USB. AIFF plays on every CDJ and in every DJ app.

items.title: Artwork that shows up
items.text: AIFF carries ID3 tags, so the cover and the comments show in rekordbox, Serato and Traktor alike.

items.title: Same sound, more room
items.text: AIFF is uncompressed, so the files are bigger than the FLACs. The sound doesn't change at all.

quality.title: Is that FLAC really lossless?

items.q: Does converting FLAC to AIFF lose quality?
items.a: No. Both are lossless, so the AIFF holds exactly the same samples as the FLAC. What changes is the container: AIFF stores the audio uncompressed.

items.q: Why are AIFF files bigger than FLAC?
items.a: FLAC compresses the audio without losing anything, the way a zip does. AIFF doesn't compress it, so at 16-bit/44.1 kHz it takes about 10 MB per minute of stereo audio.

items.q: Can I convert a whole folder at once?
items.a: Yes. Drop the folder and convert everything in one go.

items.q: Will my cue points survive?
items.a: Traktor's do: Surco moves the cues and the beatgrid to where Traktor reads them in an AIFF. rekordbox keeps its cues in its own library; load the AIFF with “Replace” and the same rekordbox row points at the new file, cues and playlists included.

items.q: Does it work on Windows?

cases.title: Add tags and artwork to a whole folder, without making copies
cases.s: Surco fills in tags and artwork in the same files, with no copies and no format change.
body: You have a folder of music with missing tags or no artwork. You want Surco to fill them in on its own, in the same files, with no copies and no format change.
Set it up once. After that, every folder takes four steps.
cases.keywords: tag tags metadata artwork cover autofill

settings.note: Off by default. When you drop your tracks, Surco looks each one up and adds its details and artwork when it is sure. If Discogs is among your sources, add its token first.
Every file keeps its format. An MP3 stays an MP3. OGG, OPUS and AAC are skipped, and an M4A comes out as ALAC.
Surco saves the changes into the same file instead of making a new one.
So you can go back to the old file if you don't like something.

steps.title: Drag the folder into Surco
steps.text: Tracks in its subfolders come in too. Surco starts looking them up on its own.

steps.title: Wait for the lookup to finish
steps.text: At the top you'll see “Auto-matching…” with a counter. Wait for it to finish.

steps.title: Check the ones left to confirm
steps.text: In the list filter, pick “To confirm”. These are the ones Surco wasn't sure about. Review them or leave them as they are.

steps.title: Click “Convert”
steps.text: It's the button in the top bar. Surco asks before touching your files. Click “Overwrite and convert”.

points: The sound doesn't change. Only the tags and artwork are written, which is why it's so fast.
Tracks you leave unconfirmed keep the tags they already had.
Traktor cue points stay where they were.

It only works on a Mac, because the swap goes through Apple Music. The old track has to be in your Apple Music library.

settings.note: That way Surco checks whether the track is already in your library.
Apple Music doesn't take FLAC. AIFF sounds the same as WAV and keeps the artwork too.

cases.title: Set up your tracks' cues with your own flow
cases.s: Mark where the track drops and your flow places the rest of the cues.
body: You prepare your rekordbox tracks the same way every time, with cues counted from where the track drops. You want to mark that point with one click, or have Surco suggest it, and have it place the rest.
This is how one DJ does it with their flow, but the point can be whatever you like and you build the flow your own way. It works on Mac and Windows.
cases.keywords: hot cues call memory drop breakdown subidón mix in bars auto mark automatic suggestions unanalyzed complete on close

settings.setting: Put a CALL where you mark
settings.note: Give your flow a name, say Subidón. Its rule already counts back from where you mark every 16 bars and places hot cue + CALL. Change “Once” to “3 times” and pick “a colour per repeat” with blue, green and red. This box, ticked by default, adds the CALL at the point.
That's the default. A is always the first cue in the track. Turn it off if each letter is a fixed pad for you.

settings.setting: When rekordbox closes, apply your active flow to tracks with CALLs and no hot cues
settings.note: To mark the point in rekordbox instead of in Surco. You put a CALL where the track drops while you prepare and, when you close rekordbox, Surco adds your flow's hot cues. Turning it on tells you how many tracks it will complete.

steps.title: Open your rekordbox playlist
steps.text: It's in Surco's sidebar, with your collection's folders. Pick a track and go to the Cues section.

steps.title: Pick your flow
steps.text: In the section's “Flow” menu, say Subidón. It stays picked for the next tracks.

steps.title: Mark where the track drops
steps.text: Hovering over the zoomed waveform shows an outline preview of what the flow would place. On click, Surco counts back from that point and places a red hot cue at 48 bars, a green one at 32 and a blue one at 16, each with its own CALL, plus a CALL at the point. If you'd rather Surco looked for it, press “Auto mark”. It suggests where the track drops, with the flow shown in outline, and you accept them all at once with Return or one by one.

steps.title: Click “Save to rekordbox”
steps.text: With rekordbox closed, it saves right away. If it's open, Surco waits and saves when you close it. Then move on to the next track.

points: Auto mark suggests, it doesn't decide. Its suggestions aren't always right, so nothing is saved until you accept them.
To prepare several at once, select them in the list and choose “Auto mark the selected”. Each row tells you how many suggestions it has, and you see them when you open it.

If rekordbox hasn't analyzed the track yet, Surco measures the tempo and the grid itself and you can set the cues without opening rekordbox. Once rekordbox analyzes it, Surco moves them onto its grid. Auto mark works too, working out where each bar starts from the changes in the bass.

When rekordbox closes, Surco only completes tracks rekordbox has already analyzed, with a CALL and no hot cues, so a track that already has hot cues stays as it is. Surco has to be open when you close rekordbox.
rekordbox takes at most 8 hot cues, A to H. If one doesn't fit, Surco tells you.
If one cue is enough, two flows come ready-made. Mix in 64 places a hot cue 16 bars before the point and Mix in 32, 8 bars before.
The cues are saved to your rekordbox collection, not to the file. Before Surco writes to it, make your own backup of the library from rekordbox. Surco makes one too.
If you just converted the track and sent it to rekordbox playlists, the rekordbox icon next to the result takes you to it in “Recently added” with its cues open.

privacy.metaDescription: What data leaves your computer when you use Surco, which services it goes to and what this website measures.
privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lede: Surco has no account and no telemetry. This is everything that leaves your computer when you use the app, and what this website measures.
privacy.privacyLede: Surco has no account and no telemetry, and sends nothing to any Surco server. The app only connects to other services in these cases.
privacyItems: When you search for a track, by hand or with auto-match, it sends the title, the artist and other search details to the sources you have turned on. These can be Discogs, Bandcamp, Deezer, Beatport and MusicBrainz. Artwork is downloaded from their servers and from Cover Art Archive.
If you connect your Beatport account, your username and password only travel to Beatport. The password is stored encrypted on your computer.
To find out whether there is a new version, it checks the releases published on GitHub and downloads the update from there.
If you report a bug, it opens a GitHub form in your browser with the version, the system and the latest error lines, without folder paths. Nothing is sent until you post it yourself.
privacy.policiesLabel: Each service has its own privacy policy
privacy.webBody: getsurco.app uses Google Analytics and Vercel Analytics to count visits and downloads. The desktop app uses neither.

stats.metaDescription: How many times Surco has been downloaded on Mac, Windows and Linux without bots, and how installs grow week by week.
stats.title: How many people download Surco
stats.lede: Surco has no telemetry, so it doesn't know who uses it. What is public is how many times each installer is downloaded from GitHub. These figures come from that.
stats.macLede: On Mac, updates come through a different file, so every download here is someone installing Surco.
stats.estimatedLegend: The dotted part is rebuilt from the date of each version. The solid part is measured every day.
stats.weeklyHeading: New installs on Mac per week
stats.updatesLede: How many Macs downloaded each update. It is the closest thing to knowing how many people really use Surco.
howItems: On Mac only the .dmg installer counts. Updates download a different file, so the two never mix.
On Windows and Linux the installer is also the update, so each new version adds one download for every person who updates.
Every version gets one or two downloads from automated programs that fetch every file. They are taken off using a file no person ever needs.
stats.measuredSince: GitHub only keeps today's total. Everything before {{date}} is rebuilt from the date of each version, and since then a snapshot is saved every day.
